newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade ministry punishes six in oil scandal.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade ministry punishes six in oil scandal.

text.p: Japan's trade minister disciplined six senior officials on Thursday for accepting favours from an oil dealer suspected of massive tax evasion in the latest blow to the prestige of Tokyo's powerful mandarins.

Trade Minister Shinji Sato singled out six Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) officials from among the 41 who have admitted to being wined and dined by a high-flying oil wholesaler arrested last month for suspected tax evasion.
Sato apologised for what he called "nothing but a lapse of discipline", but shrugged off suspicions of influence peddling by MITI officials.
"I am confident that contacts with (oil wholesaler Junichi) Izui have not distorted our oil policy," he told a news conference.
Vice MITI Minister Tsutomu Makino will have his salary cut for two months, while the five others were given strong warnings, Sato said.

The MITI disciplinary measures, the result of an internal probe of 138 officials, were announced less than 24 hours after police arrested a former top health ministry bureaucrat on suspicion of taking bribes from a nursing home operator.

Former Vice Health Minister Nobuharu Okamitsu was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of taking 60 million yen ($530,000) from Hiroshi Koyama, head of a firm which runs homes for the elderly, the Metropolitan Police Department said.
Koyama was arrested last month on suspicion of bribing another health ministry official in order to gain government subsidies for his chain of nursing homes.

For Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, the widening scandals mean both embarrassment at fresh reminders of collusion between officials and business leaders and impetus to make good on October election pledges to cut economic regulations and curb bureaucratic powers, analysts said.
"The people's trust in public administration has hit rock bottom," Seiroku Kajiyama, the government's top spokesman, told a news conference.

"At a time when both Japan and the world are looking at this country's future with a sense of crisis, the damage caused by these affairs is regrettable," he said, adding the cabinet was mulling new anti-corruption measures.

One immediate setback for Japan from the MITI oil scandal was that Sato was forced to scrap plans to attend a key World Trade Organisation ministerial conference from December 9-13 in Singapore, in order to face questions in parliament.

Although no politicians have been implicated in the health ministry and MITI scandals, the news comes as a blow to Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP), which last month formed its first cabinet without a coalition since it was driven from power after a series of scandals in 1993.

"This affair reveals that elected lawmakers have neglected their duty to citizens, who have given them the power to check bureaucratic excess," said political commentator Yoichi Masazoe. "It shows the low quality of our politicians."

For many Japanese, there was an uncomfortable sense of deja vu in the scandals, which called to mind the late 1980s "bubble economy" era of inflated asset prices, when daily headlines often carried complex, multiple scandals embroiling LDP lawmakers and businessmen.

Hashimoto has been closely associated with the health industry throughout his career and has acknowledged receiving political donations from lobbyists affiliated with Koyama, the nursing home operator accused of bribing health bureaucrats.

He headed MITI from July 1994 until he became prime minister last January -- part of the 10-year period during which the officials were treated to dinners and golf by Izui, who was arrested last month on suspicion of evading 310 million yen ($2.76 million) in taxes.
